config.title: Find Peak Element

intro.title: Find Peak Element
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that finds a peak element in an array. A peak element is defined as an element that is greater than or equal to its neighbors. You will learn to implement a binary search algorithm to solve this lesson efficiently. The main technologies involved are JavaScript arrays, loops, and conditional logic. This exercise will help you understand how to apply binary search to non-sorted data and improve your lesson-solving skills.
intro.usecase: The Find Peak Element algorithm is essential for analyzing data trends in real-world applications like financial dashboards and sensor monitoring systems. In stock trading platforms, it helps identify local price peaks to inform buy/sell decisions by analyzing historical price charts. For IoT systems monitoring temperature or pressure sensors, it detects abnormal spikes that could indicate equipment failure or security breaches. This pattern also powers features in fitness apps that identify peak performance moments during workout sessions, and in e-commerce analytics that find sales peaks during promotional campaigns.

objectives: Implement a linear scan algorithm to identify peak elements in an array
Construct a binary search approach for efficient peak detection
Initialize and manipulate pointer variables to track array indices during traversal
Apply conditional logic to compare adjacent elements and identify peaks
Configure edge case handling for arrays with single elements or boundary peaks
Integrate validation checks to ensure input array integrity
Render test cases with various array configurations to verify algorithm correctness

content.body: Have you ever looked at a mountain range and tried to spot the highest peak? In programming, we sometimes need to find a 'peak' element in an array. Let's learn how to do this efficiently using a clever memory technique.
content.title: Introduction

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
1. Explain what a peak element is in an array context
2. Apply a single-pass approach to find a peak
3. Implement the solution using a memory structure to track comparisons
4. Determine when to store and check values in your lookup
content.title: What you'll learn
Try it
content.prompt: Look at this array: [1, 3, 2]. Which element is larger than both its neighbors?
content.successMessage: Great! 3 is larger than both 1 (left) and 2 (right). That's a peak element.

content.title: Try a bigger array
content.prompt: Now look at [1, 2, 3, 1]. Which element is a peak?

content.title: One more
content.prompt: What about [1, 2, 1, 3, 5, 6, 4]? Find any peak element.
content.successMessage: Excellent! You might have found 2 (larger than 1 and 1) or 6 (larger than 5 and 4). Both are correct peaks.

content.body: What you just did was examine each element and compare it with its neighbors. For small arrays, this visual scanning works well.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When arrays have thousands of elements, checking every position against both neighbors becomes inefficient. We need a smarter approach that remembers what we've seen. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen. Instead of re-scanning the entire array, we can use a mental notebook to track comparisons as we go. For peak finding, we don't need to store every value - we just need to remember whether we're ascending or descending.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: A notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step.

content.body: We'll walk through the array once, comparing each element with the next one. If we find an element that's greater than its next neighbor, we've found a peak!
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Walkthrough with [1, 2, 3, 1]:
Start at 1 → compare with 2 (ascending, continue)
Check 2 → compare with 3 (ascending, continue)
Check 3 → compare with 1 (descending! 3 is greater than 1)
Found peak at index 2 (value 3)

content.body:
1. Start at the first element
2. Compare current element with the next one
3. If current > next, we found a peak (return it)
4. Otherwise, move to next element
5. The last element is always a peak (no next element to compare)
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Create the function
steps.instruction: Let's start by creating our function. We'll call it findPeakElement and it should take an array nums as parameter.
steps.hint: Use the function keyword or arrow function syntax.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function definition that accepts nums parameter
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've created the function structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure your function accepts a parameter called nums.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. We need a function that takes an array parameter.

steps.title: Add loop through array
steps.instruction: Now add a loop to go through the array. We need to check each element except the last one in the loop.
steps.hint: Use a for loop that goes from i = 0 to i < nums.length - 1
steps.expectedOutcome: A for loop that iterates through the array
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Now we can examine each element.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close. Make sure your loop stops before the last element.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember we need to compare each element with the next one, so we stop before the last index.

steps.title: Add peak check
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, check if the current element is greater than the next one. If it is, return the current index immediately.
steps.hint: Use an if statement comparing nums[i] > nums[i + 1]
steps.expectedOutcome: An if statement that returns i when nums[i] > nums[i + 1]
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Now we can detect peaks as we go.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Make sure you're comparing with the next element (i + 1).
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to check if current element is greater than the next one, then return the index.

steps.title: Handle the last element
steps.instruction: After the loop, return the last index. Why? Because if we never found a peak in the loop, the last element must be a peak (there's nothing after it to be smaller).
steps.hint: Add return nums.length - 1 after the loop
steps.expectedOutcome: Return statement for the last index
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Your function is now complete.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close. We need to return the index of the last element.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember, if no peak was found earlier, the last element is always a peak.

content.body: Great work! You've implemented an efficient peak-finding algorithm. Remember: the key insight was walking through the array once and returning as soon as we find a descent. This is much faster than checking every element against both neighbors. Keep practicing this 'single pass with memory' pattern - it's useful for many array lessons!
content.title: Done
